text: Most organizations classify data into the same small set of tiers, even when they call them different things. This lesson covers the common four-tier scheme, what actually distinguishes one tier from the next, and a legally distinct scheme you shouldn't confuse with it.

Public is fine for anyone to see, marketing material, published pricing. Internal is for employees, not damaging if it leaked, an org chart, a meeting agenda. Confidential would cause real harm if disclosed, customer records, unannounced financial results. Restricted is the most sensitive tier, a leak here means regulatory penalties or serious harm to the people the data describes, Social Security numbers, health records, credentials.

The label itself is just a name. What makes a tier meaningful is three questions answered consistently. Who can access it, from anyone at Public to a small named list at Restricted. What happens if it leaks, from nothing at Public to severe regulatory and personal harm at Restricted. What controls apply, from none at Public to multi-factor authentication and mandatory audit trails at Restricted.

Exact label names and tier counts vary by organization, and that's fine, as long as the scheme is small, clearly defined, and consistently applied. What's not fine is borrowing the U.S. government's Confidential, Secret, and Top Secret scheme for commercial use. That's a legally-defined national-security system administered through formal clearance, a completely different thing from a company's Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted model. Keep the two separate in your head.

You won't find these exact four labels everywhere, but you'll find some small, tiered scheme under whatever names an organization chose. The skill is recognizing the pattern. Next up: discovering sensitive data in the first place.
